item.title: Computing with Coupled Oscillator Networks: Optimization, Memory, and Modern AI Primitives
item.description: arXiv:2610.39703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Allibhoy, Fabio Pasqualetti

item.title: Steering the dynamics by controlling the temporal interaction network
item.description: arXiv:2607.04998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many real-world coupled dynamical systems have their interaction structure and strength that evolve or adapt over time. Here, we investigate how one can control the state of a system by tuning its temporal interaction network. We present a framework based on nonlinear optimal control, where one has control over the time-dependent coupling matrix of a dynamical system. We show how to obtain the gradient of the Lagrangian functional of a generic optimal control problem using the adjoint method, where the control variables are multiplicative inputs. We illustrate the theory with the precision cost that aims at steering the nodal states to prescribed target trajectories. We first focus on a linear time-variant system for which further expressions of the gradient can be obtained. Second, we uncover the temporal interaction that pushes a nonlinear neural units model towards target trajectories. For both systems, we numerically solve the optimal control problem, imposing various constraint on the structure of the controlled edges. The workflow presented here can be leveraged to steer the dynamics of systems with artificial or engineered interaction that is tunable.
item.dc:creator: Melvyn Tyloo

item.title: Paths to synchronization in the Kuramoto model with inertia
item.description: arXiv:2607.09171v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synchronization is ubiquitous across natural and synthetic systems, yet most prior studies focus on the inertia-free Kuramoto model and do so at the macroscopic level. In this study, we instead investigate the inertial Kuramoto model and analyze the kinetics of individual synchronized clusters that emerge in the underdamped dynamics, driven by the interactions among multiple synchronized clusters with different frequencies. Specifically, we explore two forms of intrinsic frequency distribution -- unimodal Gaussian and multimodal uniform -- and show that they give rise to qualitatively different synchronized clusters: a hierarchical organization for the Gaussian distribution and a homogeneous organization for the uniform distribution. This contrast leads to qualitatively different behaviors of the order parameter: for the Gaussian distribution, it increases smoothly with increasing coupling strength, while for the uniform distribution, it grows through a series of discrete jumps that trace out the size of the Devil's staircase (DS). By resolving the kinetics at the cluster level, we further find that the route to synchronization also depends on the distribution type: with a Gaussian distribution, a single dominant cluster forms and gradually entrains the remaining oscillators, whereas with a uniform distribution, synchronization proceeds via successive cluster mergers initiated from peripheral seeds associated with the high-frequency periphery. Taken together, these findings provide a new perspective on collective synchronization dynamics in inertial complex systems.
item.dc:creator: Cook Hyun Kim, Yeomoon Kim, Stefano Boccaletti, B. Kahng

item.title: Explosive Synchronization in Inertial Kuramoto Models: Determining Resilience in Power Grids
item.description: arXiv:2609.00910v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Maintaining power-grid stability is essential for a sustainable energy supply. Using empirical power-grid data, we show that the inertial Kuramoto model with correlated powers and coupling strengths provides a relevant framework for analyzing explosive synchronization and grid stability. We identify two distinct synchronization pathways, initiated by population-driven or coupling-driven seed rotors, that yield different order-parameter behaviors. Inertia, in turn, determines whether the resulting seed clusters retain distinct angular velocities. Similar mechanisms govern recovery from external disturbances, linking power-grid resilience to these two nucleation pathways. Our findings provide a microscopic framework for understanding synchronization and recovery, with implications for stable power-grid operation.
item.dc:creator: Cook Hyun Kim, Jihye Kim, Sangjoon Park, J\"urgen Kurths, B. Kahng

item.title: The limits of higher-order interactions in shaping chimera states
item.description: arXiv:2610.31997v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In neuronal networks, chimera states, characterized by the coexistence of coherent and incoherent populations, have attracted considerable attention in the study of collective brain dynamics, due to its potential implications for neurological disorders such as epilepsy. Their emergence has been extensively investigated with a particular emphasis on the role of network topology, both in conventional pairwise interactions and, more recently, in higher-order interaction networks. Here, we propose a generalized framework for neuronal hypergraphs incorporating higher-order interactions through attractive chemical and repulsive electrical coupling. Using networks of FitzHugh--Nagumo neurons with interaction orders d=2,3,4, corresponding to (d+1)-body interactions within a framework that can be extended to higher d, we numerically investigate the emergence of chimera states under the combined effect of attractive and repulsive coupling and we compare the resulting dynamics with those of their corresponding clique-projected networks. Our results reveal that, both dynamical similarities and qualitative differences between genuine higher-order interactions on hypergraphs and their pairwise representations. While higher-order interactions often support broader chimera regions, we show that clique projections can also preserve or promote chimera states, even in regimes where the corresponding hypergraphs exhibit fully incoherent dynamics. Therefore, these findings suggest that chimera formation is not only influenced by the topology or by the interaction order but also by the form of the coupling functions and the balance between attractive and repulsive interactions, offering further insights into collective dynamics in neuronal networks.
item.dc:creator: Ediline L. F. Nguessap, Thierry Njougouo, Fernando Fagundes Ferreira

item.title: CrowdEgress: A Multi-Agent Simulation Platform for Pedestrian Crowd
item.description: arXiv:2406.08190v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This article introduces a simulation platform to study complex crowd behavior in social context. The agent-based model is extended based on the social force model, and it mainly describes how agents interact with each other, and also with surrounding facilities such as walls, doors and exits. The simulation platform is compatible to FDS+Evac, and the input data in FDS+Evac could be imported into our simulation platform to create single-floor compartment geometry, and a flow solver is used to generate the roadmap towards exits. Most importantly, we plan to integrate advanced social and psychological theory into our simulation platform, especially investigating human behavior in emergency evacuation,such as pre-evacuation behavior, exit-selection activities, social group and herding effect and so forth.
item.dc:creator: Peng Wang, Xiaoda Wang, Peter Luh, Neal Olderman, Christian Wilkie, Timo Korhonen

item.title: Prospective Coding and Path Integration Emerge as Equilibrium Solutions of Self-Organizing Neural Networks with Firing-Rate Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2606.14649v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continuous Attractor Neural Networks (CANNs) traditionally rely on pre-wired recurrent connectivity to model spatial representations, path integration, and anticipatory dynamics. However, the biological mechanisms through which this structured connectivity emerges via learning remain relatively unexplored. This work presents a theoretical framework revealing how continuous attractor connectivity and its computational properties self-organize through Hebbian plasticity, firing-rate adaptation, and global inhibition. We show that translationally invariant inputs naturally drive the emergence of stable, Gaussian-profiled feedforward weights. Crucially, anticipatory dynamics arise spontaneously within these feedforward architectures, shifting the activity bump forward without requiring recurrent excitatory collaterals. This predictive shift can be linearly amplified across multilayer networks, consistent with anticipatory activity observed in the superficial layers of the entorhinal cortex. Furthermore, introducing recurrent interactions allows the network to learn connections capable of self-sustaining a moving bump of activity. Finally, by modulating the network with an external, time-varying baseline current that encodes speed, the system adjusts its intrinsic velocity to function as a precise unidirectional path integrator. Ultimately, this study suggests that prospective coding and path integration are not manually engineered features, but rather naturally co-emergent properties of a single self-organizing competitive network.
item.dc:creator: Facundo Emina, Emilio Kropff

item.title: Altered temporal scaling of semantic similarity fluctuations in psychosis
item.description: arXiv:2606.23043v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scale-free temporal organization, in which fluctuations show similar statistical structures across timescales, is a feature of many complex systems considered to support optimal functioning. Alterations of such scaling have been reported in several pathologies, but whether comparable alterations characterize the temporal organization of language remains largely unexplored. We address this question in the domain of psychosis, where language anomalies are pervasively documented. Specifically, we apply detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) to quantify temporal scaling in Qwen3-derived continuous cosine similarity time series, capturing trajectories through semantic space computed from transcripts of picture descriptions across three independent datasets. DFA scaling exponents {\alpha} were extracted to characterize the strength of long-range temporal correlations. Across all datasets, patients exhibited significantly elevated {\alpha} relative to controls, indicating increased temporal persistence in semantic fluctuations. This analysis opens a window into the multi-timescale organization of meaning as it unfolds in discourse and reveals a signature of altered temporal scaling. This alteration parallels known departures from critical scaling in brain dynamics in psychosis, suggesting the exploration of possible links between these two.
item.dc:creator: Paola Moreno Ancalmo, Irem Topal, Emre Bora, Rieke Roxanne M\"ulfarth, Svenja Seuffert, Tilo Kircher, Frederike Stein, Philipp Homan, Wolfram Hinzen
